entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To spread from one person to another; used about illnesses, rumors, stories and jokes.
entries.usage: Very common in the progressive: *There's a bug going around*, *A rumor is going around that …* It is intransitive, the subject is the illness or the rumor, and a place can follow: *going around the office*. British speakers also say *go round*.
entries.pattern: there's a bug / the flu going around; a rumor is going around (that …)
examples: Half my class is out sick. There's a stomach bug **going around**.
A rumor is **going around** that the coffee shop on the corner is closing.
A joke about the new parking rules has been **going around** the office all week.

drill.sentence: Let's keep the baby home this week; a nasty cold is {{going around}} at daycare.
drill.hint: passing from person to person (not *spreading*)

entries.related: *spread* — more general and formal; *circulate* — formal, for rumors, documents and emails; *catch something* — get an illness from someone.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To have serious difficulty dealing with something, such as a task, a skill, an illness or a feeling.
entries.usage: Very common and neutral: *struggle with math, depression, the new software, a decision*. It is inseparable and often in the progressive; *struggle to* + verb is also common: *struggle to pay the rent*. It sounds more serious than *have trouble with*, and people use it kindly about others' difficulties.
entries.pattern: struggle with + noun; struggle to + verb
examples: My son **struggles with** reading, so we work with a tutor twice a week.
A lot of first-year college students **struggle with** homesickness.
After the accident, he **struggled with** anxiety every time he got in a car.

drill.sentence: I've always {{struggled with}} public speaking; my hands shake before every toast.
drill.hint: found very hard (not *had trouble with* or *had a hard time with*)

entries.related: *have trouble with* — lighter; *cope with* — manage a difficult situation; *wrestle with* — think hard about a problem or decision.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To get an advantage or help from something, such as a change, a program or an experience.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in news, health advice and reports: *benefit from exercise, a tax break, more sleep*. The person who gains is the subject, and the source follows *from*. For the other direction, use *benefit* + object: *The new park will benefit the whole neighborhood.*
entries.pattern: benefit from + noun / -ing; X benefits someone
examples: Kids **benefit from** playing outside every day, even when it's cold.
Small businesses will **benefit from** the new tax break, according to the city.
Our team really **benefited from** having a designer in the room early on.

drill.sentence: Your knee will {{benefit from}} a few weeks of physical therapy.
drill.hint: be helped by (not *improve with*)

mistake.wrong: Everyone can benefit of a good night's sleep.
mistake.right: Everyone can benefit from a good night's sleep.
mistake.why: The verb *benefit* takes *from*; *of* goes with the noun, as in *the benefit of*.

entries.related: *profit from* — more about money, or sounds calculating; *gain from* — similar, neutral; *take advantage of* — use a chance, sometimes unfairly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make progress, or to decide to go ahead with a plan, project or decision.
entries.usage: Common in business, news and official statements: *The city will move forward with the new stadium.* At work, *Moving forward, …* is often used to mean from now on, and some people find it jargon. In personal life it means continue after a hard time: *It's time to move forward.*
entries.pattern: move forward (with a plan / a project / a decision)
examples: The school board voted to **move forward with** plans for a new swimming pool.
We can't **move forward** until the client signs the contract.
After a hard year, she was ready to **move forward** with her life.

drill.sentence: The city council approved the budget, so the park renovation can finally {{move forward}}.
drill.hint: advance to the next stage (not *go ahead* or *proceed*)

entries.related: *go ahead with* — start a planned action; *proceed with* — formal; *move on* — stop dealing with something and start something new.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start to work well and form a satisfying whole, after the separate parts did not fit yet.
entries.usage: Common for plans, projects, teams, meals and rooms: *The plan is finally coming together.* It is intransitive and often in the progressive with *finally* or *really*. It also means gather or unite (*The town came together after the fire*), which is a different sense.
entries.pattern: X is (finally) coming together; it all came together
examples: After weeks of rehearsals, the play is finally **coming together**.
Once we added the rug and some plants, the living room really **came together**.
The team struggled early in the season, but everything **came together** in the playoffs.

drill.sentence: The sauce tasted strange at first, but after an hour on the stove, it all {{came together}}.
drill.hint: started to work as a whole (not *worked out* or *fell into place*)

entries.related: *fall into place* — happen in the right way; *work out* — end well; *click* — informal, suddenly start working well.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To sleep later than usual in the morning, usually on purpose.
entries.usage: Very common and relaxed: *I'm going to sleep in on Saturday.* It is intransitive and usually describes a pleasant choice; for an accident that makes you late, Americans usually say *oversleep*. British speakers also say *have a lie-in*.
entries.pattern: sleep in (on Saturday / on the weekend)
examples: It's Saturday, so I'm going to **sleep in** and make pancakes later.
The kids were up late at the party, so we let them **sleep in**.
I love hotels with late checkout because I can **sleep in** on vacation.

drill.sentence: I don't have to be at work until noon tomorrow, so I can {{sleep in}}.
drill.hint: stay in bed later than usual, on purpose (not *oversleep*)

mistake.wrong: On Sundays I like to sleep long.
mistake.right: On Sundays I like to sleep in.
mistake.why: *Sleep long* sounds unnatural for this idea; natives say *sleep in* or *sleep late*.

entries.related: *sleep late* — same meaning; *oversleep* — sleep too long by accident; *have a lie-in* — British.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stay somewhere a little longer than planned, often to wait for something or to keep someone company.
entries.usage: Informal and friendly: *Stick around for dessert*, *Can you stick around after class?* It is intransitive; add *for* + noun or *to* + verb. It can also mean stay in a job or a place over time: *I don't think he'll stick around for long.*
entries.pattern: stick around (for dinner / to help / after class)
examples: Why don't you **stick around** for dinner? There's plenty of food.
If you **stick around** after the show, the band usually comes out to sign autographs.
Can you **stick around** for a few minutes after class? I want to talk about your essay.

drill.sentence: The fireworks start at nine, so {{stick around}} if you want to see them.
drill.hint: stay a bit longer (not *stay* or *hang out*)

entries.related: *hang around* — stay somewhere with no clear purpose; *stay put* — not move from where you are; *stick with someone* — stay close to them or stay loyal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To avoid becoming involved in something, such as an argument, someone else's problem or a fight.
entries.usage: Common as advice or a sharp request: *Stay out of it!*, *I try to stay out of family drama.* It is inseparable, and the object follows *of*; *Stay out of my business* sounds rude. It also means keep away from a place: *stay out of the sun*.
entries.pattern: stay out of it / an argument / someone's business
examples: When my parents argue about money, I just **stay out of** it.
Most of my coworkers **stay out of** office politics, but Dan loves the drama.
On our street, neighbors mostly **stay out of** each other's business.

drill.sentence: It's not your fight, so {{stay out of}} it and let them work it out themselves.
drill.hint: don't get involved in (not *keep out of*)

entries.related: *keep out of* — very similar; *get involved in* — the opposite; *butt in* — interrupt or get involved when you are not wanted.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To help someone, especially for a short time or with a practical task, often when they are busy or in trouble.
entries.usage: Very common in speech: *help out at the food bank*, *help out with the kids*. It works with or without an object; a pronoun goes in the middle (*Can you help me out?*), and a noun can go on either side of *out*. It sounds more casual and practical than *help* and often suggests a favor.
entries.pattern: help out (with something / at a place); help someone out
examples: My mom comes over on Tuesdays to **help out** with the twins.
Thanks for **helping** me **out** last weekend. I couldn't have moved that couch alone.
A lot of high school students **help out** at the food bank over the holidays.

drill.sentence: We're short on volunteers for the bake sale. Could you {{help out}} for a couple of hours on Saturday?
drill.hint: give practical support (not *pitch in* or *lend a hand*)

entries.related: *pitch in* — join others to help with a shared task; *lend a hand* — help, often physically; *chip in* — give money or help as part of a group.

entries.label: phrase (feel + left out)
entries.meaning: To feel sad or hurt because other people are not including you in their activities or conversations.
entries.usage: Very common when talking about kids, friends, siblings and coworkers. *Left out* is the past participle of *leave someone out*, so you can also say *be left out* or *Don't leave her out.* *So nobody feels left out* is a common phrase when inviting a whole group.
entries.pattern: feel left out (of something); be left out
examples: Invite the whole class to the party, so nobody **feels left out**.
When my coworkers talk about fantasy football at lunch, I kind of **feel left out**.
Older kids can **feel left out** when a new baby arrives.

drill.sentence: My two best friends planned a weekend trip and didn't invite me, so I {{felt left out}}.
drill.hint: was sad not to be included (not *excluded*)

entries.related: *feel excluded* — more formal; *be left out* — not be included, a fact rather than a feeling; *fit in* — the opposite, feel part of the group.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop hoping that someone will improve or change, or that something will succeed, and stop trying to help.
entries.usage: Common in talk about family, students, relationships, teams and plans: *Don't give up on me.* It is inseparable, and the person or thing follows *on*. Compare *give up* + noun or *-ing*, which means stop doing something: *give up smoking*.
entries.pattern: give up on someone / a plan / a dream
examples: Most of his teachers had **given up on** him, but one coach still believed in him.
Please don't **give up on** me. I'm really trying to change.
I'd almost **given up on** my tomato plants when they suddenly started producing.

drill.sentence: Even after three losing seasons, the fans never {{gave up on}} the team.
drill.hint: stopped believing in (not *lost faith in*)

entries.related: *lose faith in* — stop trusting; *write someone off* — decide someone will fail; *stand by someone* — the opposite, stay loyal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To look or behave like the people or things around you, so that you are not noticed.
entries.usage: Used for people in new places, tourists, animals, colors and buildings: *blend in with the locals*. It is intransitive; add *with* for the group or the background. The opposite is *stand out*.
entries.pattern: blend in (with the locals / the crowd / the background)
examples: I wore a plain gray hoodie so I'd **blend in** with the other students.
Tourists in white sneakers and fanny packs don't exactly **blend in**.
Arctic foxes turn white in winter to **blend in** with the snow.

drill.sentence: On my first day at the new school, I just wanted to {{blend in}} and not be noticed.
drill.hint: look like everyone else (not *fit in*)

entries.related: *fit in* — be accepted as part of a group; *stand out* — the opposite; *keep a low profile* — avoid attention.

entries.label: verb pattern
entries.meaning: To plan or intend to do something, often to buy, sell, hire or move soon.
entries.usage: Very common in business, real estate and job talk: *We're looking to hire*, *Are you looking to buy or rent?* In this sense it is almost always in the progressive and followed by *to* + verb. It sounds more casual and less fixed than *plan to* or *intend to*.
entries.pattern: be looking to + verb (buy / sell / hire / move)
examples: We're **looking to** hire two more nurses before the winter.
Are you **looking to** buy a car this month, or just browsing?
My sister's **looking to** move closer to our parents next year.

drill.sentence: The owners of the bakery are {{looking to}} sell the business and retire to Florida.
drill.hint: intending (not *planning*, *hoping* or *trying*)

entries.related: *plan to* — more definite; *intend to* — formal; *be thinking of* + *-ing* — less certain.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something next, after finishing something else, especially as the next stage in a life or career.
entries.usage: Common in biographies, news and stories: *She went on to win three Olympic medals.* It is followed by *to* + verb and often links a modest start with later success. Compare *go on* + *-ing*, which means continue the same activity.
entries.pattern: go on to + verb (win / become / found …)
examples: She started as a cashier and **went on to** run the whole company.
Many of the kids from that summer camp **went on to** play college basketball.
After a slow first half, the home team **went on to** win by twenty points.

drill.sentence: Her first novel sold only a few hundred copies, but she {{went on to}} write three bestsellers.
drill.hint: did later, as the next stage of her career

mistake.wrong: He studied medicine and then went on becoming a famous surgeon.
mistake.right: He studied medicine and then went on to become a famous surgeon.
mistake.why: For the next step in a sequence, use *go on to* + verb; *go on* + *-ing* means continue doing the same thing.

entries.related: *end up* + *-ing* — finally be in a situation, often unplanned; *go on* + *-ing* — continue; *later* — a simple adverb, less narrative.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To stop thinking about a disagreement or a feeling for now, so that it does not get in the way of something more important.
entries.usage: Typical with *differences*, *pride*, *feelings* and *personal opinions*: *Let's put our differences aside for the kids.* A noun object can go before or after *aside*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *put it aside*. It also means save money for later, like *set aside*.
entries.pattern: put aside your differences / pride / feelings; put it aside
examples: For one night, the two brothers **put aside** their differences and celebrated their dad's birthday.
I had to **put** my pride **aside** and ask my neighbor for help.
The two competing pizza places **put aside** their rivalry for a day to cook for flood victims.

drill.sentence: For their daughter's sake, her parents agreed to {{put aside}} their anger and sit together at her graduation.
drill.hint: not let it get in the way, for now (not *forget* or *let go of*)

entries.related: *set aside* — same in this sense, slightly more formal; *let go of* — stop holding on to a feeling for good; *bury the hatchet* — make peace after a long fight.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To meet someone, usually in person, to discuss something important in a serious and focused way.
entries.usage: Common at work, in families and in journalism: *sit down with your manager, a financial planner, the kids*. It suggests a planned, unhurried conversation, and journalists use it for interviews: *We sat down with the director.* The noun *sit-down* (*a sit-down with the boss*) is informal.
entries.pattern: sit down with someone (to talk about / discuss something)
examples: I need to **sit down with** my boss and talk about my workload.
Before we buy a house, we should **sit down with** a financial planner.
This week, we **sat down with** the author to talk about her new novel.

drill.sentence: Before the kids start middle school, we should {{sit down with}} them and talk about phones and social media.
drill.hint: have a serious, planned talk with (not *talk to*)

entries.related: *meet with* — more formal, common in American business; *have a word with* — a short, private talk; *catch up with* — talk about recent news.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be considered or accepted as a particular thing, according to rules or to common opinion.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, especially in questions and jokes: *Does cereal count as dinner?* It is intransitive, and a noun or an adjective follows *as*: *Does this count as healthy?* Without *as*, *count* alone means matter: *Every little bit counts.*
entries.pattern: X counts as + noun / adjective
examples: Walking the dog doesn't really **count as** exercise, does it?
Two years of part-time work **counts as** one year of experience for this job.
Does a video call really **count as** a first date?

drill.sentence: I'm not sure a single slice of tomato on a burger {{counts as}} eating your vegetables.
drill.hint: is accepted as (not *qualifies as*)

entries.related: *qualify as* — more formal, meet the official conditions; *be considered* — neutral, often passive; *pass for* — be mistaken for something else.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be the opposite of a rule, principle, belief or someone's wishes, or to act against them.
entries.usage: Common with *the rules, my principles, everything I believe in, your parents' wishes, your instincts*. It is inseparable; the subject can be an action (*That goes against the rules*) or a person (*She went against her doctor's advice*). *Go against the grain* is an idiom for doing the opposite of what is normal.
entries.pattern: go against the rules / your principles / someone's wishes
examples: Lying to a customer **goes against** everything I believe in.
She **went against** her parents' wishes and became a chef instead of a lawyer.
Painting your front door purple **goes against** the homeowners' association rules, apparently.

drill.sentence: I know it's cheaper, but buying from that company {{goes against}} my principles.
drill.hint: conflicts with (not *violates*)

entries.related: *violate* — formal, break a rule or law; *go against the grain* — be unusual or unnatural; *go along with* — the opposite, accept or agree.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be caused by something or to develop from it.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in news, psychology and analysis: *The problem stems from poor communication.* The result is the subject, and the cause follows *from*. It is intransitive, so it has no passive form.
entries.pattern: result + stems from + cause
examples: A lot of his anger **stems from** a difficult childhood.
The delivery delays **stem from** a shortage of truck drivers.
Most of my stress **stems from** trying to please everyone.

drill.sentence: The fight between the two neighbors {{stems from}} an argument over a fence fifteen years ago.
drill.hint: grew out of and was caused by (not *dates back to*, *goes back to* or *comes from*)

mistake.wrong: Most of their arguments are stemmed from money.
mistake.right: Most of their arguments stem from money.
mistake.why: *Stem from* is intransitive, so it has no passive form.

entries.related: *come from* — informal, more general; *arise from* — formal; *result from* — similar, focused on the outcome.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To cause something to start suddenly, such as an alarm, an explosion, a reaction or a series of events.
entries.usage: Common with *alarms, fireworks, an allergy, a chain reaction, panic*: *Steam from the shower set off the alarm.* A noun object can go before or after *off*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *set it off*. With a person as object it means make them suddenly angry or upset: *Don't set him off.*
entries.pattern: set off an alarm / fireworks / a reaction; set it off
examples: Smoke from the oven **set off** the fire alarm in the whole building.
Cats **set off** my allergies, so I can't stay at my sister's place for long.
The announcement **set off** a wave of panic buying at grocery stores.

drill.sentence: A raccoon in the garage {{set off}} our car alarm in the middle of the night.
drill.hint: caused to start ringing (not *triggered* or *tripped*)

entries.related: *trigger* — very similar, more formal; *spark* — start a reaction or a debate; *set off* without an object — start a journey.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To cause something to happen, especially a change or an important result.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in news, history and serious discussion: *bring about change, reform, a shift*. A noun object usually follows *about*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *What brought it about?* It sounds more formal than *cause* and is usually used for big or long-term changes.
entries.pattern: bring about change / a shift / reform
examples: The new principal **brought about** real changes in how the school handles bullying.
What **brought about** the sudden change in his attitude?
The arrival of the railroad **brought about** huge changes in small Western towns.

drill.sentence: Years of hard work by local volunteers finally {{brought about}} a cleaner, safer river.
drill.hint: caused to happen (not *led to* or *resulted in*)

entries.related: *cause* — neutral, often for bad results; *lead to* — more common in speech; *effect change* — formal, bring about change.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To leave a room, building or desk for a short time, planning to come back soon.
entries.usage: Common at work and on the phone, often as a polite explanation: *He just stepped out; can I take a message?* It is intransitive; add *for* + a purpose or *of* + the room: *step out of the meeting*. It sounds softer and more polite than *leave*.
entries.pattern: step out (for a minute / for some air / of the meeting)
examples: Sorry, Dr. Chen just **stepped out**. Can I take a message?
I'm going to **step out** for some fresh air. I'll be right back.
Our host **stepped out** to grab more ice, so make yourselves at home.

drill.sentence: Mom's not here right now. She {{stepped out}} to pick up a few things at the store.
drill.hint: left for a short time (not *ran out* or *went out*)

entries.related: *pop out* — informal, more British; *run out* — leave quickly for an errand; *step away* — leave your desk or a conversation for a moment.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To wait for something, such as news, a decision or a delivery, before you can act or continue.
entries.usage: Informal and mostly American: *We're waiting on the landlord*, *I'm still waiting on a callback.* It is common in speech and work chat, but some careful speakers see it as nonstandard and prefer *wait for*. *Wait on someone* also means serve them, as in a restaurant.
entries.pattern: be waiting on a decision / an answer / someone
examples: We're still **waiting on** the roofer's estimate before we can decide.
Dinner's ready; we're just **waiting on** your dad.
The project is stuck because we're **waiting on** approval from the legal team.

drill.sentence: I can't book the flights yet because I'm still {{waiting on}} my boss to approve my vacation days.
drill.hint: depending on, before I can act (informal US; the standard verb uses *for*)

entries.related: *wait for* — standard in all registers; *hold off* — delay an action on purpose; *wait on someone* — serve them, as a waiter does.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To schedule a meeting, an event or a person for a certain time, knowing that the plan may still change.
entries.usage: Common in work and social planning: *Let's pencil in Tuesday*, *I'll pencil you in for three.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*pencil you in*), and a noun can go before or after *in*. The image is writing in pencil so you can erase it later, unlike a confirmed plan.
entries.pattern: pencil someone in (for a time); pencil in a date
examples: I'll **pencil** you **in** for Thursday at two, and you can call if anything changes.
Let's **pencil in** dinner with your parents for the weekend after next.
The band has **penciled in** a fall tour, but the dates aren't final yet.

drill.sentence: I'm not sure I'll be back in time, but {{pencil me in}} for Saturday's game and I'll confirm on Friday.
drill.hint: put me on the schedule for now (not *count me in* or *put me down*)

entries.related: *schedule* — neutral, more fixed; *book* — make a firm arrangement; *tentatively* — formal adverb for the same idea: *tentatively scheduled*.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To change a meeting, deadline or event to an earlier date or time.
entries.usage: Common in American work and planning talk: *move up the deadline, the wedding, my appointment*. A noun object can go before or after *up*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *move it up*. British speakers more often say *bring forward*, and the opposite is *push back*.
entries.pattern: move up a meeting / a deadline / a date; move it up
examples: The dentist had a cancellation, so they **moved** my appointment **up** to Tuesday.
Because of the storm forecast, the league **moved up** Saturday's games to Friday night.
They **moved** the wedding **up** to June so her grandmother could be there.

drill.sentence: My sister's doctor thinks the baby will come early, so we {{moved up}} the baby shower by two weeks.
drill.hint: changed to an earlier date (not *brought forward*)

entries.related: *bring forward* — the British equivalent; *push back* — make later; *reschedule* — neutral, earlier or later.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To mark an item on a list, usually with a check mark, to show that it is done or present.
entries.usage: Common in American English: *check off items on a to-do list, names on a list*. A noun object can go before or after *off*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *check it off*. British speakers more often say *tick off*, which in American English means make someone angry.
entries.pattern: check off an item / a name (on a list); check it off
examples: There's nothing more satisfying than **checking off** the last thing on my to-do list.
The teacher **checked off** each kid's name as they got on the bus.
We've **checked off** three national parks this year, and Yellowstone is next.

drill.sentence: Each time you finish a chore, {{check it off}} the list on the fridge.
drill.hint: mark it as done (not *cross it off* or *tick it off*)

entries.related: *cross something off* — draw a line through it; *tick off* — British for check off; *ticked off* — American informal for angry.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To deal with a problem or a painful feeling slowly, step by step, until it is solved or you feel better.
entries.usage: Common in talk about grief, relationship problems, therapy and difficult tasks: *work through your feelings, our issues, a backlog*. It is inseparable: the object follows *through*, even a pronoun (*work through it*), and *with* + a person is common: *work through it with a counselor*. It suggests patient effort rather than a quick fix.
entries.pattern: work through grief / problems / feelings (with someone)
examples: It took her two years of therapy to **work through** her grief after her brother died.
Every couple has problems; what matters is that you **work through** them together.
I'm slowly **working through** a huge pile of emails from my vacation.

drill.sentence: Our son was bullied at his old school, and a counselor is helping him {{work through}} his anger.
drill.hint: slowly come to terms with (not *process*, *deal with* or *get over*)

entries.related: *get through* — survive a hard period; *process* — understand and accept an emotional event; *get over* — recover from something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become so excited or involved in something that you lose control and do or say too much.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, often with *a little* or *a bit*, as an apology or a warning: *Sorry, I got carried away*, *Don't get carried away.* It is intransitive; add *with* or *by* for the cause: *get carried away with the decorations*. It usually sounds light and forgiving, not seriously critical.
entries.pattern: get (a little) carried away (with something)
examples: I meant to buy one plant, but I **got carried away** and came home with twelve.
Sorry, I **got carried away**. I just love talking about old cars.
Some fans **got carried away** after the win and tore down the goalposts.

drill.sentence: Let's keep the party small this year. Last time we {{got carried away}} and invited half the town.
drill.hint: became so excited we lost control (not *went overboard*)

entries.related: *go overboard* — do too much, especially spending; *get worked up* — become upset or angry; *lose your head* — stop thinking clearly.

entries.label: adjective phrase
entries.meaning: To be annoyed, unhappy and tired of a situation, a person or a thing that has continued for too long.
entries.usage: Informal and common in complaints: *I'm fed up with the noise, my job, waiting*. It takes *with* + noun or *-ing*; *fed up of* is common in British speech but sounds wrong to many Americans. It often leads to a decision: *I got fed up and quit.*
entries.pattern: be / get fed up with + noun / -ing
examples: I'm **fed up with** my phone dying by lunchtime every day.
After years of long commutes, she finally **got fed up** and moved closer to work.
Commuters are **fed up with** the constant delays on the Red Line.

drill.sentence: We're {{fed up with}} the neighbors' dog barking at five every morning.
drill.hint: annoyed and tired of (not *sick of* or *tired of*)

entries.related: *sick of* or *sick and tired of* — very similar, informal; *tired of* — milder; *have had it with* — informal, at the end of your patience.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make someone feel sad, tired or discouraged, especially over a period of time.
entries.usage: Informal and common in speech, often with weather, work or bad news as the subject: *This rain is getting me down.* The person always goes between *get* and *down* (*It gets me down*), and the negative is common as advice: *Don't let it get you down.*
entries.pattern: X gets someone down; Don't let it get you down.
examples: All this gray weather is really **getting** me **down**.
Don't let one rejection **get** you **down**; every writer gets dozens.
Being stuck at home with a broken leg started to **get** him **down** after a few weeks.

drill.sentence: The players have lost eight straight games, and it's starting to {{get them down}}.
drill.hint: make them sad and discouraged (not *wear on them*)

entries.related: *bring someone down* — similar, also about a mood; *depress* — stronger; *cheer someone up* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start to have an illness, usually a common one such as a cold, the flu or a fever.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and work messages: *I think I'm coming down with something.* It is inseparable; the illness follows *with*, and the progressive suggests the illness is just starting. It is used for common, short illnesses, not for serious long-term diseases.
entries.pattern: come down with a cold / the flu / something
examples: I think I'm **coming down with** a cold. My throat's been sore all day.
Half the wedding guests **came down with** food poisoning the next day.
Our pediatrician says a lot of kids are **coming down with** strep this month.

drill.sentence: Can we move our lunch to next week? I feel like I'm {{coming down with}} the flu.
drill.hint: starting to get sick with (not *catching* or *getting*)

entries.related: *catch* — get an illness from someone; *fight off* — avoid getting sick; *be under the weather* — feel slightly ill.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To manage to live or do something with just enough money, knowledge or skill, but not more.
entries.usage: Common in talk about money and languages: *We get by on one salary*, *I can get by in Spanish.* It is intransitive; add *on* + an amount of money or *with* + what you have. It suggests the situation is hard but not desperate.
entries.pattern: get by (on one salary / with a little Spanish)
examples: When the kids were little, we **got by** on one salary and a lot of pasta.
My Italian isn't great, but I can **get by** in restaurants and shops.
Lots of college students **get by** on instant noodles and free pizza.

drill.sentence: Rent went up again, and a lot of families in our building are barely {{getting by}}.
drill.hint: managing with just enough money (not *scraping by* or *making ends meet*)

entries.related: *make ends meet* — have just enough money for basics; *scrape by* — get by with great difficulty; *manage* — more general.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To eat, drink, use or do less of something, usually for health or money reasons, without stopping completely.
entries.usage: Very common in health and money advice: *cut down on sugar, coffee, screen time, spending*. It is inseparable, and *on* comes before the thing you reduce. *Cut back on* means almost the same; *cut something out* means stop completely.
entries.pattern: cut down on sugar / coffee / screen time
examples: If you **cut down on** sugar, you'll have more energy in the afternoon.
Our school is trying to **cut down on** paper, so report cards now come by email.
I've **cut down on** social media, and I honestly feel happier.

drill.sentence: Ever since his heart scare, my dad has been trying to {{cut down on}} red meat and fried food.
drill.hint: eat less of (not *cut back on*)

entries.related: *cut back on* — very similar, common for spending; *reduce* — formal; *cut out* — stop completely.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To stop eating, using or doing something completely, often for health reasons.
entries.usage: Common in health and diet talk: *cut out sugar, gluten, alcohol, caffeine*. A noun object can go before or after *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *cut it out*. As an exclamation, *Cut it out!* means stop doing that, especially to children or friends.
entries.pattern: cut out sugar / soda / caffeine; Cut it out!
examples: Since I **cut out** soda, my headaches have mostly gone away.
To save for the trip, we **cut out** restaurants completely for three months.
I **cut** sugar **out** of my coffee, and after a week I didn't miss it.

drill.sentence: The dermatologist suggested I {{cut out}} dairy for a few weeks to see if my skin improves.
drill.hint: stop having completely (not *give up* or *quit*)

entries.related: *cut down on* — have less, not none; *give up* — stop a habit; *eliminate* — formal, common in diet advice.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To increase the size, amount or reach of something, such as production, a business or a program.
entries.usage: Common in business, tech, science and public programs: *scale up production, a pilot program, operations*. A noun object usually follows *up*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *scale it up*. It suggests a planned step from small to large; the opposite is *scale back* or *scale down*.
entries.pattern: scale up production / a program / a recipe; scale it up
examples: The bakery started with one oven and **scaled up** to supply forty grocery stores.
If the pilot program works, the city plans to **scale** it **up** to every neighborhood.
You can easily **scale up** this recipe if you're cooking for a crowd.

drill.sentence: The startup makes great sneakers, but it doesn't have the money to {{scale up}} production yet.
drill.hint: increase to a much larger size (not *ramp up* or *expand*)

entries.related: *ramp up* — increase quickly; *expand* — general; *scale back* — reduce.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To join with another person or group to work on something together, often for one project.
entries.usage: Common in news, business, sports and everyday talk: *Two neighbors teamed up to clean the park.* It is intransitive; add *with* + the partner, and *to* + verb or *on* + the project. It suggests an equal partnership for a specific goal.
entries.pattern: team up (with someone) (to do something / on something)
examples: Two local chefs **teamed up** to open a taco truck downtown.
For the science fair, Mia **teamed up with** her best friend.
The city has **teamed up with** a bike-share company to add a hundred new stations.

drill.sentence: My brother and I {{teamed up}} on a surprise video for our parents' fortieth anniversary.
drill.hint: worked together as partners (not *joined forces* or *partnered*)

entries.related: *join forces* — similar, a little more formal; *partner with* — common in business; *collaborate* — formal, often for creative or research work.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To manage without something you need or want.
entries.usage: Common with *can't*, *could* and *have to*: *I can't do without my morning coffee*, *We'll have to do without.* It can take an object or stand alone at the end of a sentence. *I could do without* is a common ironic phrase for something you would prefer not to have: *I could do without the drama.*
entries.pattern: can't do without + noun; have to do without; I could do without …
examples: We had to **do without** hot water for three days while they fixed the pipes.
I can't **do without** my phone when I'm traveling.
I could **do without** my neighbor's leaf blower at seven on a Sunday morning.

drill.sentence: We couldn't afford a car for years, so we learned to {{do without}} one.
drill.hint: manage with none (the verb is not *live* or *go*)

entries.related: *go without* — not have something, often food or sleep; *manage without* — neutral; *make do with* — manage with less than you want.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something useful for your community or society, such as volunteering or donating, often because you feel you have received a lot.
entries.usage: Very common in American interviews, speeches and company statements: *give back to the community*. In this sense it is intransitive, usually with *to*; separable *give something back* simply means return it. It sounds sincere, though in corporate messages it can sound like a cliché.
entries.pattern: give back (to the community / to your hometown)
examples: After retiring, he started tutoring kids at the library as a way to **give back**.
The basketball star opened a free clinic in his hometown to **give back** to the community.
Our company gives every employee two paid days a year to volunteer and **give back**.

drill.sentence: She got help from a local food pantry as a kid, and now she volunteers there every week to {{give back}}.
drill.hint: repay her community by helping others (not *pay it forward* or *help out*)

entries.related: *pay it forward* — help others because someone helped you; *volunteer* — work for free; *donate* — give money or things.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To keep money over a period of time so that you can buy something specific later.
entries.usage: Common in everyday speech: *save up for a car, a trip, a house*. It is usually intransitive with *for* + noun or *to* + verb (*saving up to buy a house*), but you can also *save up* an amount: *I saved up five hundred dollars.* *Up* stresses gradual saving toward a goal; *save* alone is more general.
entries.pattern: save up for + noun; save up to + verb
examples: My son is **saving up for** a new bike, so he's mowing lawns all summer.
We **saved up** for two years to take the kids to Japan.
Many young couples **save up** for a down payment by living with their parents.

drill.sentence: I've been {{saving up}} for months, and I finally have enough for a new laptop.
drill.hint: keeping money bit by bit toward a goal (not *putting money aside*)

entries.related: *put aside* or *set aside* — keep money for a purpose; *save* — more general; *splurge* — the opposite, spend a lot at once.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To compare prices or offers from several sellers or providers before you buy or decide.
entries.usage: Common in advice about insurance, mortgages, cars and phone plans: *It pays to shop around.* It is intransitive; add *for* + what you want: *shop around for a better rate*. It works for services too: *shop around for a new dentist*.
entries.pattern: shop around (for a better rate / a contractor)
examples: Before you renew your car insurance, **shop around**. You could save a few hundred dollars.
We **shopped around for** a contractor and got five very different quotes.
Patients often don't know they can **shop around for** cheaper blood tests.

drill.sentence: Prices for the same TV can differ by two hundred dollars between stores, so it pays to {{shop around}}.
drill.hint: compare offers before buying (the verb is not *look*)

entries.related: *compare prices* — plainer; *look around* — browse; *comparison shopping* — the American noun phrase for this activity.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To choose one thing or person from a group, usually with care.
entries.usage: Common for clothes, gifts, furniture, colors and pets: *pick out a dress, a puppy, paint colors*. A noun object can go before or after *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *Did you pick it out yourself?* It can also mean recognize someone in a group: *She picked him out of a lineup.*
entries.pattern: pick out a gift / an outfit / a color; pick it out
examples: My daughter **picked out** her own outfit for the first day of school.
We spent an hour at the shelter before we **picked out** a puppy.
Did you **pick out** this wine? It's really good.

drill.sentence: We let my mom {{pick out}} the paint colors for the new kitchen, and they look great.
drill.hint: select from the options (not *choose*)

entries.related: *choose* — neutral; *select* — formal; *pick up* — a different verb: lift or collect.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To use or test something for a short time to see whether it works or whether you like it.
entries.usage: Common for products, recipes, restaurants, apps and new ideas: *try out a new recipe, the new gym, a different route*. A noun object can go before or after *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *try it out*. *Try out for* a team or a play means compete for a place in it.
entries.pattern: try out a recipe / a product / a place; try it out
examples: I **tried out** the new Thai place on Elm Street last night, and the curry was amazing.
Most bike shops let you **try** a bike **out** before you buy it.
The city is **trying out** car-free Sundays on Main Street this summer.

drill.sentence: The store lets you {{try out}} the mattress for a hundred nights, and you can return it if you don't like it.
drill.hint: use it as a test (not *test*)

entries.related: *test* — more formal or technical; *try on* — for clothes; *try out for* — compete for a place on a team.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To watch or listen to a TV or radio program, a live stream or a podcast, especially at the time it is broadcast.
entries.usage: Common in broadcasting language: *Tune in next week*, *Millions tuned in to watch the final.* It is intransitive; add *to* + the program or channel, or *to* + verb. It is most common for live events such as sports, news and award shows.
entries.pattern: tune in (to a show / a station); tune in to watch
examples: More than a hundred million people **tuned in** to watch the Super Bowl.
**Tune in** tomorrow at seven for part two of our interview.
My grandpa **tunes in to** the local radio station every morning for the weather.

drill.sentence: The whole family {{tuned in}} to see my cousin compete on the cooking show.
drill.hint: switched on the TV for the broadcast (not *watched*)

entries.related: *watch* or *listen to* — plain verbs, for any time; *stream* — watch online; *tune out* — stop paying attention.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To appear or happen suddenly or unexpectedly.
entries.usage: Informal and very common for ads, messages, problems, new businesses and people: *An error message popped up*, *Coffee shops are popping up everywhere.* It is intransitive. The adjective *pop-up* describes something temporary or sudden: *a pop-up store*, *a pop-up ad*.
entries.pattern: X pops up (on the screen / everywhere / out of nowhere)
examples: After a week of rain, mushrooms **popped up** all over the backyard.
Every time I open that website, an annoying ad **pops up**.
Our old neighbor **popped up** on a game show last night. We couldn't believe it.

drill.sentence: Every few months, a new problem {{pops up}} with this old car.
drill.hint: suddenly appears (not *crops up* or *comes up*)

entries.related: *come up* — happen unexpectedly, for problems and events; *show up* — arrive; *crop up* — appear unexpectedly, mostly for problems.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To die; a gentle, polite way of saying it.
entries.usage: Used when talking to or about the family of someone who died, in condolence messages and in announcements: *Her father passed away last spring.* It is intransitive and is used for people, sometimes for pets. Many Americans also say just *passed*: *My grandmother passed in June.*
entries.pattern: pass away (peacefully / last year / at the age of …)
examples: My grandfather **passed away** peacefully in his sleep last year.
I'm so sorry to hear that your mom **passed away**.
The founder of the bakery **passed away** at ninety-two, and the whole town came to the funeral.

drill.sentence: We were sad to hear that our old piano teacher had {{passed away}} over the winter.
drill.hint: a gentle way to say *died* (not the form with *on*)

entries.related: *die* — neutral and direct; *lose someone* — *We lost my uncle last year*; *pass on* — another polite form, less common.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To suddenly become unconscious for a short time; to faint.
entries.usage: Common in everyday speech about heat, blood, shock, alcohol and exhaustion: *I almost passed out when I saw the bill.* It is intransitive. Informally, it can also mean fall asleep very quickly from exhaustion, and separable *pass something out* means hand it out.
entries.pattern: pass out (from the heat / at the sight of blood)
examples: It was so hot at the parade that two people **passed out**.
I always feel like I'm going to **pass out** when they take my blood.
A runner **passed out** just before the finish line, but medics got to her quickly.

drill.sentence: She hadn't eaten all day, and she nearly {{passed out}} during her spin class.
drill.hint: lost consciousness (not *fainted* or *blacked out*)

entries.related: *faint* — same, a little more formal; *black out* — lose consciousness or memory; *come to* — wake up again after passing out.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To try to impress people by showing them how good, rich or clever you are, in a way others often find annoying.
entries.usage: Usually critical: *Stop showing off!*, *He's just showing off.* With an object (*show off a new car, your cooking*), it means display something proudly and is less negative; a pronoun goes in the middle: *show it off*. A person who does this is a *show-off*.
entries.pattern: show off (for someone); show off a new car / a skill
examples: My nephew kept **showing off** on his skateboard until he fell and scraped his knee.
She loves to **show off** her cooking when we have guests over.
Ignore him. He's just **showing off** for his friends.

drill.sentence: You don't need to use big words in every sentence. People will think you're {{showing off}}.
drill.hint: trying to impress everyone (not *bragging*)

entries.related: *brag* — talk proudly about yourself; *flaunt* — show something off in an obvious, annoying way; *humble* — the opposite quality.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start living a calm, stable life in one place, often by getting married, buying a home or having children.
entries.usage: Common in talk about life plans, often as *get married and settle down*. It is intransitive; add *in* + a place or *with* + a partner. It can sound a little traditional, and it also means become calm: *Settle down, kids!*
entries.pattern: settle down (in a place / with someone)
examples: After ten years of moving around for work, they finally **settled down** in a small town in Vermont.
My parents keep asking when I'm going to **settle down** and have kids.
A lot of young professionals leave the city once they're ready to **settle down**.

drill.sentence: She spent her twenties traveling and working abroad, and at thirty-five she was ready to {{settle down}}.
drill.hint: start a stable, quiet life in one place

entries.related: *put down roots* — make a place your permanent home; *settle in* — get used to a new place; *calm down* — the other sense, become calm.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become comfortable and used to a new home, job, school or situation.
entries.usage: Common in friendly questions and messages: *Are you settling in OK?*, *How's she settling in at her new school?* It is intransitive (*settle in at work*), and *settle into* + noun is a common variant: *settle into a new routine*. *Get settled* means the same.
entries.pattern: settle in (at a new job / school); settle into + noun
examples: How are you **settling in** at the new job?
It took our cat about a week to **settle in** after the move.
Most freshmen **settle in** by the end of the first semester.

drill.sentence: Our new neighbors just moved here from Texas, so let's give them a few weeks to {{settle in}} before we throw a party.
drill.hint: get comfortable in their new home (not *adjust* or *get settled*)

entries.related: *adjust* — get used to a change; *get settled* — same, often about unpacking; *settle down* — start a stable life.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To wrongly think that one person or thing is another, or to confuse two things.
entries.usage: Very common in speech: *I always mix up their names*, *I mixed up the dates.* A noun object can go before or after *up*, a pronoun goes in the middle (*mix them up*), and *mix A up with B* names both. The noun *mix-up* means a small mistake caused by confusion: *a mix-up at the airport*.
entries.pattern: mix up names / dates; mix A up with B; mix them up
examples: Sorry, I **mixed up** the dates. I thought dinner was on Friday.
The pharmacy **mixed up** my prescription with someone else's.
People often **mix** me **up** with my sister because we sound the same on the phone.

drill.sentence: The hotel {{mixed up}} our reservation with another family's, so we ended up in a room with one bed.
drill.hint: wrongly took one for the other (not *confused*)

mistake.wrong: The twins look so alike that I always mix up them.
mistake.right: The twins look so alike that I always mix them up.
mistake.why: With a pronoun object, the pronoun must go between *mix* and *up*.

entries.related: *confuse* — more formal; *get mixed up* — become confused; *mistake A for B* — think that A is B.
